title: Working as a printer in New Orleans and meeting Buddy Petit and Arnold Metoyer
summary: White talks his way into a job at Garnier's print shop, prices the work, prints for musicians, and meets Buddy Petit and Arnold Metoyer.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: How many of you are in New Orleans? Yeah.

So I walked up Rampart Street one day after I bought my first new suit after getting out of the service. Born Art Clothing Store. You know where Born Art is there. And, uh... And I got on the other side of just a little up from Poitras. And, uh, I saw this printing office. Allies Printery. And the door was open. A young lady was sitting behind the desk. Her name was Mary Dupree. And, uh, an elderly, stoop-shouldered white man was at the desk and he was covering some papers. And so I just forced myself. I walked in and I said, how do you do, sir? And so, Miss Dupree, she got up and said, can I help you? And I told her, I said, well, I'm a printer and I'm kind of looking around to find a job someplace. She said, Mr. Garnier, Mr. Garnier, here's a printer. And Mary said to me, we've been looking for a printer. I saw the office and it was a well-equipped office. There were three job presses. There was a linotype machine sitting here. There was a cylinder back there. There were stones. There was planning machines. There were stones over here. And chasers and everything. And such a big, fine printing office. I looked and I said, you don't have any printer here? Mr. Garnier said, no, I don't have no printer here, no. You know, he talked like Creole. And he was a Creole. Garnier. He said, I look for a printer, but I want a good printer, he said. I said, well, I'm a good printer. How long have you been working at the trade? I said, I haven't been working at the trade. I said, I'm just out of the army. He said, if you're just out of the army, you don't print it. You don't print it. I said, well, you try me. He said, I got three jobs here to put up. He sold me three throwaways. And he says, I want these jobs out. And I suppose this was long about 11 o'clock in the day.
I said, the case here, you have to find a type.

I said, I'll find them. So I dropped around and then I scanned out faces here. And the cases were laid out in series, you see. I set up one six by nine in all series. I set up another six by nine in all series. I set up another in all series. And he had plenty of type. Find this equipped job shop in New Orleans, boy. Not to be busy. I throw these three handbills on one after one. Thousands of each of them. And when he came back around four o'clock, all the jobs were stacked up there and ready for me. He looked at me. Where you learn your printing? I said, in Jenkins Orpens in Charleston, South Carolina. My God. I said, man, you're a good printer.
He said, how much do you think that would? I said, well, about, say, six dollars a thousand. Oh, no, no, no, no.
I get a dollar half a thousand from him. I said, oh, you can't work with me. You got a dollar half a thousand.

You got a dollar half a thousand. You can't get. I said, the paper costs more than that. How much you want to work for me? He said, I said, $25 a week. You make the price on the job and everything? I said, I'll price all the jobs. You give the people good work? I said, I'll give them good work. Where you learn estimating at? I said, I've had charge of the job department of the Charleston Metro ever since I was a boy. I said, I can price my job, and I can price the stock, and I'll give you a profit. I said, but if I make it, you must pay me. He said, you talk mighty big. You must know what you do. I said, well, I'm a big man. Little shrimp, you know. He looked at me, cut my arm, said, good boy, you go to work. He said, you price the job. Mary, he said, you take his orders. So Mary was a very beaten young girl. She come up from St. Martinsville, Paris, down there, fine-looking, beautiful girl. And we had no relationship other than a business way, but she was all business. She had graduated from that college down there under Professor somebody, Turo or somebody. They had a business college down there in the Pithian Temple that taught these girls typing and business acumen. And she was very good. She kept an account of everybody. I said, all six by nines are $6.50 a thousand. All calling cards are $2.25 per hundred, $4.50, $5.00, $7.50 a thousand. I set the price. She said, you gonna be in competition with the boy up Dryad Street? And I said, okay, I wanna do better work than they're doing. And I did. And I started printing the contracts with the musicians. The first musician I met was Buddy Petit. And Buddy Petit came in there and he stopped, I want some cards printed. He said, can I get them today? I said, sure you can get them today. My name is Buddy Petit, he said. I said, my name is Amos Mordecai White. So you a printer here? I said, yeah. I printed some bills around here where it says Buddy Petit's band, so you a musician, aren't you? Yeah, I'm a musician. I'm a trumpet player. I'm here, I'm a trumpet player. So he had his claridad player with him. What did you call that boy? Zeb. Zeb. Zeb was with him. And he's having him start bragging on themselves. I said, good, good. I said, that's fine. And then I was glad to meet him. I said, but let me get your card in there. And if they talk right on, I'm putting the card up for him. So while he was waiting there, I printed the cards for him. One hundred. Oh, and Buddy took a light to me. You play music too? I said, yes, I'm just out of the army. I'm a former bandmaster in the army. Yeah? So he started telling the boys all around town. So they started coming in there to get their printing done. You see? Next fellow I met down there was Arnold Matoia. He dropped in one day along with Lizzie. And Lizzie said, I'm going to bring him up on the Temple roof garden tonight. So I don't have any horn. They took my horn from me. Took my own horn from me in the army. I had a whole, I mean I had a york trumpet that I carried in the service with me. And they took that too. And of course the army band instruments had all USA stamped on them, you see. And mine wasn't stamped, but it happened so now. They wouldn't have taken mine. But mine was in the material. Army band material. All that we had stacked up and allowed to put away. And mine was all that. And I intend to pick up my cornet and bring it along with me. And to my surprise the things that we did.
